preamble: 3 2 1 22 9 7 (whose clues may be partial) begins a limerick which ends: Got a mouthful of pips, And threw himself into the sea.

clue.text: Howdah dissipated derisive sound, bagatelle before a strong piece

indicators.note: before places the bagatelle piece ahead of what follows it
dissipated means scattered, so the letters of the word Howdah are scattered into a new order

parts.note: a raspberry is a rude noise blown with the tongue to show derision
a bagatelle is a trifle, something of little importance
the forte is the strong part of a sword blade, nearest the hilt

explanation.surface: An elephant's seat falls apart amid jeers, and a trivial game comes before a powerful item.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble supplies the definition: this is the second line of the limerick. 'dissipated' rearranges HOWDAH as WHOHAD. The clue is partial, so it reads as a string of pieces rather than a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these lights together form a line of the limerick about the man from Torquay who ate a dessert at teatime.

clue.text: See 3
The first plate from Alrewas, an almond cocktail, at ground level on alternative stage

annotationWithheld.why: The first plate from Alrewas, an almond cocktail, at ground level on alternative stage: THE + ALREWAS less A (first) and L (plate) + AN + OLDMAN (anagram of almond) gives THEREWASANOLDMAN, but no honest reading of 'at ground level on' gives the OFT before OR (alternative) + QUAY (stage)
annotationWithheld.clue: The first plate from Alrewas, an almond cocktail, at ground level on alternative stage

clue.text: Stir a fool 9, perhaps

parts.note: git is British slang for a stupid or contemptible person
the answer to 9-across, for tea, suggests what was eaten at that meal, so had for tea gives ate

explanation.surface: An instruction to stir an idiot into something, the fool being an example of the answer to 9.
explanation.walkthrough: 9-across is FORTEA, from the limerick line 'who had raspberry trifle for tea'; what you have for tea you ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To agitate a liquid is to stir or shake it vigorously, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Mercian's present sound

indicators.note: sound tells you the word for a present is to be said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: to offer something is to present it

explanation.surface: A man from Mercia is said to have a gift for the current sound.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was the eighth-century King of Mercia, the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of central England known for Offa's Dyke.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, so he was its most famous inhabitant.

clue.text: Problem arising among Christian symbols — make fateful decision

indicators.note: among puts the problem phrase in the middle of the Christian symbols

parts.note: a cross and an icon are both symbols of the Christian faith
from Hamlet's 'there's the rub', the rub is the difficulty that arises

explanation.surface: A difficulty appears among the crosses and images of a church, and someone has to choose a course of action.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'symbols' supplies two separate Christian emblems, and 'among' sets the Hamlet phrase between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar crossing the river Rubicon committed him to civil war, so the phrase means taking an irrevocable step.

clue.text: Philosophies (nothing less) need reform (the man began to say)

indicators.note: reform means reshape, so the remaining letters plus need are put into a new order
less signals taking something away from the word Philosophies

parts.note: nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Schools of thought, with nothing removed, are in need of reform, as a man begins to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the limerick's next line. 'less' removes an O from PHILOSOPHIES, and 'reform' shuffles PHILSOPHIES with NEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening one's mouth to speak is starting to talk, which fits the bracketed description of the man beginning to say something.

clue.text: Walker round house follows doctor all the way

indicators.note: follows places the walker piece after the doctor piece

parts.note: Doctor Who is the time traveller of the BBC science fiction series

indicators.note: round means the walker piece goes around the house abbreviation

parts.note: a leg is what you walk with

explanation.surface: Someone out walking circles a building, coming after a medic, and goes the full distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walker' looks like a person on foot, but it is the limb used for walking; 'round' wraps it around the house abbreviation, after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Going the whole hog is an idiom for doing something thoroughly, so the phrase means all the way.

clue.text: See 1
Contributor to crossword finds alternative to reason at its top

annotationWithheld.why: Contributor to crossword finds alternative to reason at its top: RHYME (as in rhyme or reason) + R, but the R can only come from the top of 'reason', which is already used to give RHYME, so one word does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Contributor to crossword finds alternative to reason at its top

clue.text: Patterns used in church

indicators.note: used means worked over or worn, so the letters of the word Patterns are reworked

explanation.surface: Designs found on the inside of a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests decorative designs used in church, but 'used' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is the crosswise arm of a cross-shaped church, so it is found in church.

clue.text: Ideal spot for the dentist

indicators.note: for here means the answer is supplied by the run of letters within the dentist

explanation.surface: A perfect place for someone who fixes teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are concealed across the words 'the dentist'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden of Eden is the biblical paradise, so its name stands for any perfect place.

clue.text: Would-be re-purchaser of books — "___ like a ___" in bleak midwinter

definitions.meaning: Tim ..., founder of the ... bookshop chain, tried to buy the business back after selling it
the carol In the Bleak Midwinter has the line 'earth stood hard as iron, water like a stone'

explanation.surface: A businessman hoping to buy back his book chain, and a gap-fill from a Christmas carol.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterstones is a British chain of bookshops; In the Bleak Midwinter is a Christina Rossetti poem sung as a carol.
explanation.definitionFit: The bookseller's surname, and the two words that fill the blanks of the carol line, spell the same letters.

clue.text: Downward movement concerning diplomatic staff

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in business letters
a legation is a diplomatic mission and its staff, ranking below an embassy

explanation.surface: A fall in status involving the people who work at a foreign mission.
explanation.walkthrough: In British football, relegation is a team's drop to a lower division.
explanation.definitionFit: Relegation is being moved down to a lower rank or division, a downward movement.

clue.text: Fliers and swimmers don't seem respectable

parts.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, is made up of fliers
fish are creatures that swim

explanation.surface: Airmen and sea creatures who look rather disreputable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase in the surface but reads as describing someone who looks disreputable.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffish means rakish and slightly disreputable, which is how someone looks who does not seem respectable.

clue.text: End of Jewish sentence for a female re-admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the re piece goes inside a lady

parts.note: a lady is a woman
re taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman readmitted to finish a Jewish prison term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enough already' and similar Yiddish-influenced English sentences end on this word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Yiddish-influenced American English the word is tacked on at the close of a sentence for emphasis, as in enough already.

clue.text: It's very cold in S-Spain

parts.note: S taken as written from the stammered start
Iberia is the peninsula that holds Spain, and Spain's airline

explanation.surface: Someone stammering complains of the freezing weather in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter 'S-Spain' provides an extra S before IBERIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Siberia is the Russian region known for bitter winters, so it is a byword for a very cold place.

clue.text: Putting into post not as good as expected, dismissing

indicators.note: read as dis missing, the word tells you those three letters are dropped

parts.note: something that falls short of expectations is a let-down

explanation.surface: Making an appointment that disappoints and involves firing someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissing' splits as DIS + missing, so DIS is removed from the front of DISAPPOINTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Appointing someone is giving them a job or position, putting them into a post.

clue.text: Things combined to express accusation of folly

indicators.note: to express means said out loud, so the words of the accusation are heard rather than read

parts.note: calling someone a fool to their face: you nit

explanation.surface: Joined objects used to voice the charge of being foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You nit' is a mild British insult, nit meaning a silly person.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single whole made up of parts brought together, things combined into one.

clue.text: Search noisily around water for cause of tsunami

indicators.note: around means the search piece wraps the water piece
noisily means the search word is to be heard, so its sound is spelt another way

parts.note: to seek is to search
aqua is Latin for water

explanation.surface: Hunting loudly around the water for what sets off a giant wave.
explanation.walkthrough: SEEK said aloud is spelt SEKE here, and AQUA goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaquake is an earthquake beneath the sea floor, which can set off a tsunami.

clue.text: Bill's the man that's suffering

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: Bill is the person in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache is a continuous pain, a form of suffering.

clue.text: See 1
It's drawn from the bar

indicators.note: from means the letters are drawn out of the bar and rearranged

explanation.surface: Something taken from a pub counter, like a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: A breath is drawn, as a pint is drawn from the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: We speak of drawing breath, so breath is a thing that is drawn.

clue.text: Is odd room at pub the same shape?

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters of the word room are put in a strange order

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: A question whether a peculiar room in a pub has the same form as another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' turns ROOM into OMOR, and 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An isomorph is something having the same form or crystal structure as another, a thing of the same shape.
